_about: Concept ladder for the Learn stage. One concept per rung. Rung ids are progress keys: never rename. skills are glossary.json ids that move to Practiced when the check is passed. goals maps checkpoint data-ids to the rungs (1-based) that teach them.

rungs.title: Variables and types
rungs.builds: Variables: storing a number (Phase 1): int, declaring, assigning and %d. Session 1: var(1.8f) printed 1.
rungs.why: Your game has to remember things: a score, how fast the player moves, which key was pressed, whether they’re still alive. In C you say what kind of thing each variable holds before you use it. Put a different kind of value in and C converts it, sometimes losing part of it.

parts: More than one kind of box

In Variables: storing a number every box held an int. A type tells C two things about a box: what kind of value fits in it, and how to do maths with it. Phase 2 adds four more.

  • int: whole numbers. Things you count: score, lives, frames.
  • float and double: numbers with a decimal point. Things you measure: speed, position, time.
  • char: one character, like a key the player pressed.
  • bool: true or false. Alive, paused, won.
float and double

Both hold decimals. A float keeps about 6 or 7 digits, a double about 15. A plain 2.5 in your code is a double. Add an f and 2.5f is a float.

float speed = 2.5f;     // a float, exactly as written
double gravity = 9.81;  // a double
int lives = 2.9f;       // lives is 2: the .9 is chopped

Putting a decimal into an int doesn't round. C drops everything after the point.
char is a small number

A char is a one-byte number. The character in single quotes is just a friendlier way to write it: 'q' is stored as 113 and 'A' as 65. So 'A' + 1 is 66, which is 'B'. Single quotes hold one character. Double quotes, "q", make a string, which is a different thing you'll meet in Phase 3.
bool, briefly

Add #include <stdbool.h> and you get bool, true and false. Underneath, true is 1 and false is 0, so %d prints them as numbers. Comparisons, &&, || and ! tells the full story. Newer code written for C23 doesn't need the include, because bool became a built-in word.
Naming a number with #define

A number like 3 sitting in the middle of your code says nothing. Is it lives? Lanes? Give it a name:

#define MAX_LIVES 3
#define LANE_W (10 + 2)

Before the compiler reads your file, every MAX_LIVES is swapped for 3, like find-and-replace. There's no = and no ;, and the name is in capitals by habit so you can spot it. Change the 3 once and every use follows.

Put brackets round anything that's a sum. Without them, LANE_W * 2 would become 10 + 2 * 2, which is 14, not 24. And watch out for #define HALF (1/2): that's 0, because both sides are whole numbers. Division, remainder and casts explains why. Write 0.5f instead.
Mistakes MSVC catches

Same rules as before: declare a variable before you use it, or you get C2065 (undeclared identifier), and give it a value before you read it, or you get C4700. float x, y = 0.0f; still sets only y.

Two warnings are new with decimals. float speed = 1.8; squeezes a double into a float and loses a tiny bit: C4305. (A value a float can hold exactly, like 2.5, gets no warning, so don't rely on the compiler to catch every missing f.) int lives = 2.9f; chops a float into an int: C4244. Under /WX both stop the build. Add the f, or a cast (Division, remainder and casts) if you really mean it.

walk: stdbool.h gives you bool, true and false. Without it, C doesn’t know those words.
int: whole numbers only. Things you count. Starts at 0 here.
float: numbers with a decimal point. Things you measure. The f says “this number is a float”.
char: one character, in single quotes. Inside, it’s a small number (q is 113).
bool: true or false. Perfect for alive, paused, won.
Read the right side first: take score (0), add 10, put 10 back in score.

A float going into an int. An int can’t hold .9, so it gets cut off. (int) is a cast: it tells the compiler you meant it. Leave it out and MSVC warns C4244, which /WX turns into a failed build. Casts get their own concept in Division, remainder and casts. Same chop as var(1.8f) in Session 1.
Two %d slots, filled left to right by score and lives.
The other three boxes, each in its own slot: 2.5, q, and 1 for true.
rungs.model: Mental model: each variable is a box with a shape cut in the lid. C will push a value through the wrong lid without stopping you: a float squeezed into an int-shaped box loses whatever doesn’t fit, and C doesn’t round. It chops.

check.hint: Look at line 11. What happens to the part after the decimal point?
check.why: score becomes 10. lives gets 2.9 chopped to 2, never rounded up to 3. The (int) cast is you saying you meant it; without it, /W4 warns C4244 on line 11 and /WX stops the build.

miss.0: lives is an int, so it can’t hold .9. And %d prints whole numbers only.
miss.1: Close, but C never rounds when it converts to int. It drops everything after the point.
miss.3: It compiles: the (int) cast tells MSVC the chop is on purpose, so there’s no C4244.

tryit.task: Pick the type for each variable. Then print all four in one program (%f %c %d %d) and check each value comes out the way you put it in.

qa: Why 2.5f and not just 2.5?

A plain 2.5 is a double, a bigger kind of decimal. Putting it in a float squeezes it. If the value can't be stored exactly, like 1.8, MSVC warns with C4305; 2.5 happens to fit, so it gets no warning. The f makes it a float from the start either way.
How big can an int get?
On your compiler, about ±2.1 billion. Plenty for a score. How big a number can be shows the exact limits, and how to check any type's size with sizeof.
Is a char really a number?
Yes. 'q' is stored as 113. Printing values with printf shows it both ways.
Which type for which game data?
Positions, speed and delta time are float. Health, score, lives and frame counts are int. A key pressed is a char. Alive or paused is a bool. Use double only when you need extra precision.
Why does 0.1f + 0.2f not print exactly 0.3?

Floats are stored in binary, and 0.1 has no exact binary form, just like 1/3 has no exact decimal form. You get the closest value the float can hold. That's why you never test a float for being exactly 0.3. For games it's fine: nobody can see a millionth of a pixel.
rungs.bridge: You can store values. Next: printing them with printf, because %d only works for ints.

rungs.title: Printing values with printf
rungs.builds: Variables and types: the four types. Phase 1: %d and %%.
rungs.why: You can already print an int with %d. Every type gets its own slot in printf. Use the wrong slot and printf prints nonsense without stopping, so matching them is on you.

parts: How a format string works

The text in quotes is the format string. printf copies it to the screen character by character until it meets a %. That starts a conversion specification: a slot that ends at a letter such as d or f. printf takes the next value after the comma, turns it into text in the style the letter asks for, and prints that instead. That turning-into-text is why it's called a conversion.

The slot can be filled by anything that has a value, including a sum: printf("%d\n", score + bonus); prints the total without storing it anywhere.
One letter per type

• %d: an int.
  • %f: a float or double, six decimals by default.
  • %c: a char, shown as its character.
  • %e: a decimal in scientific style: 1234.5 prints as 1.234500e+03.
  • %g: 6 significant digits, trailing zeros dropped, switching to %e style for very big or very small numbers: 2.5 prints as 2.5, 1234567.0 as 1.23457e+06.
Width: lining things up

A number between % and the letter is a minimum width. %5d pads the number with spaces on the left until it fills 5 characters, so a column of scores lines up on the right. A minus sign, %-5d, pads on the right instead. A leading zero, %03d, pads with zeros: 7 prints as 007.

printf("%02d:%02d\n", minutes, seconds);   // 01:05
printf("[%5d]\n", score);                // [  120]

Width is a minimum, never a limit. A number too big for it is printed in full and simply pushes the line out.
Precision: how many decimals

A dot and a number set the precision. %.2f prints two decimals. printf rounds here, so 72.456 with %.1f shows 72.5. That's different from storing a float in an int, which chops. Width and precision combine: %8.2f means two decimals, padded to 8 characters.
Mistakes and MSVC checks

printf trusts you. If the slot says %d and you hand it a float, it reads the wrong bytes and prints a nonsense number. MSVC checks the format string against the values for you:

Too few values is C4473, too many is C4474, and a value of the wrong type is C4477. Under /WX each one stops the build. That's a gift: it turns a silent garbage number into a clear error.

Bigger types such as long long need an extra letter in the slot, like %lld. Those wait for How big a number can be.

walk: %d: the int slot. You know this one.
%f: the float slot. Prints six decimal places by default: 2.500000.
%.1f: same slot, but “only 1 decimal place”. Prints 2.5. The number after the dot is how many places.
%c: the char slot. Shows the character: q.
Same char, int slot. %d shows the number hiding inside the char.
rungs.model: Mental model: a form with differently shaped holes. printf fills them left to right. The shape of each hole has to match what you drop in.

check.hint: Variables and types said a char is a small number underneath. Which slot shows the letter, and which shows the number?
check.why: %d asks for the number, so you see 113, the code for lowercase q. %c would show the letter.

miss.1: That’s what %c would print. %d shows the number underneath.
miss.2: The char isn’t empty. It holds q, which is 113.
miss.3: Printing a char with %d is fine. A char is a small int.

tryit.task: Fill the blank so this prints HP: 72.5% (one decimal place, then a percent sign).

qa: What if I use %d for a float?
You get a garbage number, and with /W4 MSVC warns C4477 that the slot and the value don’t match. Treat that warning as a bug.
Why does %f work for a double too?
printf turns every float into a double before it prints, so %f covers both. scanf is stricter: a double needs %lf there.
How do I print a timer like 01:05?
Width 2, padded with zeros: printf("%02d:%02d\n", minutes, seconds);. Without the 0 you'd get 1: 5.
rungs.bridge: You can print anything you store. Next: reading what the player types, so the numbers come from them instead of you.

rungs.title: Reading input with scanf
rungs.builds: Printing values with printf: format slots. scanf uses the same slots, in the other direction.
rungs.why: printf talks to the player. scanf listens. It waits for them to type something and press Enter, then puts what they typed into one of your variables. It’s how the guessing game in Decisions & Loops will read a guess.

parts: The idea

scanf is printf in reverse. printf turns a number into text for the screen. scanf takes the text the player typed, turns it into a number, and stores it in your variable. That's why it needs &: it has to know where the box is so it can put something in it.
Where the typing goes

Keys the player presses don't go straight to your program. They wait in a queue called the input buffer, and nothing is handed over until Enter is pressed. Enter itself goes in the queue too, as a newline. Then scanf("%d", &lives) works through the queue like this:

  1. Skip any spaces, tabs and newlines at the front.
  2. Read characters that can be part of a whole number: digits, and a sign at the start.
  3. Stop at the first character that can't, and leave it in the queue.
  4. Turn the digits into a number and store it in lives.

Whatever is left stays in the queue for the next scanf. At the very least that's the newline from Enter.
When the player types something odd

Type 23abc and scanf reads 23, stores it, and leaves abc waiting. The next %d trips over those letters straight away.

Type abc first and step 2 finds no digits at all. scanf stores nothing, so your variable keeps whatever it had, and the letters stay in the queue. Every later %d hits the same letters and fails the same way. Once you can repeat code, that's how a program gets stuck asking forever.

To tell these cases apart, scanf returns a number: how many slots it filled. int got = scanf("%d", &lives); sets got to 1 when it worked, 0 when the first thing typed wasn't a number, and EOF (a negative number) when the input has ended. Acting on that number needs Decisions with if / else, and the full retry pattern is in do, break, continue and the endless loop.
Reading several values

One scanf can fill several slots: scanf("%d %d", &x, &y). A space in the format means “skip any amount of blank space here, even none”, so the player can type 3 4 on one line or press Enter between them.

Any other character in the format must be typed exactly. "%d/%d" reads 3/4. If the player types 3 / 4, scanf reads the 3, expects a /, sees a space and stops, returning 1.

Never end the format with \n. In scanf it doesn't mean “newline”. It means “skip blank space”, and scanf keeps skipping until something that isn't blank shows up. Your program seems frozen after Enter, waiting for you to type something else.
The letters for each type

%d reads an int and %f a float. A double needs %lf. printf can use %f for both, because it only reads the value. scanf writes into your box, so it has to know whether the box holds 4 bytes or 8.

%c is the odd one out: it doesn't skip blank space, because a space or newline is a character too. Write " %c", with a space first, to skip the newline left over from the last answer.
MSVC and Windows notes

MSVC calls scanf unsafe (C4996), and /WX turns that into a stopped build. The #define _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS line at the top, before any include, switches that warning off.

The warning suggests scanf_s. Don't just add _s to existing calls: for %c and strings, scanf_s needs an extra size number after each address, and code that skips it can crash. It also comes from an optional part of the C standard that almost only Microsoft ships.

Forget the & and MSVC warns C4477, so the build stops. To end input on purpose, press Ctrl+Z and then Enter: scanf returns EOF. On Mac and Linux it's Ctrl+D.

walk: #define lines run before the compiler reads your code. Variables and types used #define to name a number; this one flips a switch instead: it stops MSVC calling scanf “unsafe”, which with /WX would stop the build (C4996). It must come before any #include.
An int with no value yet. That’s fine, because scanf is about to fill it.
A char for the y or n answer.
No \n at the end, so the cursor waits on the same line as the question.
%d means “read a whole number”. &guess means “put it in guess”. The & gives scanf the variable’s location.
Now guess holds whatever the player typed.
" %c" reads one character. The space before %c skips the Enter still waiting from the last answer. Without it, again would grab that Enter and the question would seem to be skipped.
rungs.model: Mental model: printf needs the value to show it. scanf needs to know where the variable lives, so it can put something in it. The & means “the address of this variable”. Phase 3.5 explains addresses properly; for now, scanf always needs & before the name.

check.q: The player types 7 and presses Enter. What’s on screen after line 10?
check.hint: Line 8 has no \n. Where does the cursor sit while the player types?
check.why: The 7 appears right after the question, on the same line, because line 8 didn’t end with \n. Enter moves to the next line, and line 10 prints the result.

miss.0: scanf waits for the player before line 10 runs, so guess holds 7 by then.
miss.1: That would need a \n at the end of line 8.
miss.2: The & is code, not text. printf prints the value of guess.

tryit.task: Add a question that reads the player’s speed as a float and prints it with one decimal place.

qa: What happens if I forget the &?

With your build.bat it won’t compile: MSVC warns that %d needs an address (C4477) and /WX stops the build. Without /WX it compiles, then usually crashes when you type a number, because scanf writes to a random place in memory. One of the most common C bugs, so break it on purpose once.
What if they type letters instead of a number?
scanf stops at the first letter, stores nothing, and returns 0. The letters stay waiting for the next scanf. Checking that return value needs Decisions with if / else.
Why isn’t there a space before %d?
%d already skips spaces and Enters before a number. %c is the one that doesn’t, because a space or Enter is a character too.
Can I read a double?
Yes, with %lf. %f into a double is a type mismatch: MSVC warns C4477 and the value comes out wrong.
rungs.bridge: Your program can ask and listen. Next: Division, remainder and casts, so the numbers the player types turn into the right results.

rungs.title: Division, remainder and casts
rungs.builds: Variables and types: the float-to-int chop. The same chop hides inside division. Reading input with scanf: from now on the numbers can come from the player.
rungs.why: Timers, averages and percentages all divide. C divides two ints as ints and throws the remainder away, with no warning. Knowing when that happens saves hours of “why is this 0?”.

parts: The rule

The types going in decide the type coming out. Divide an int by an int and you get an int: the fraction is thrown away, toward zero, with no warning. 7 / 2 is 3 and 60 / 100 is 0. Bring a float in on either side, before the division happens, and the maths is done in float.

A cast, a type name in brackets like (float)hits, converts one value for this calculation: (float)7 / 2 is 3.5.
Which operator goes first

C has an order, called precedence. Casts and a minus sign in front of a number go first, then * / %, then + -. So base + level * 2 multiplies first, as you'd expect from school.

When two operators have the same rank, they run left to right. That rule is called associativity. 100 / 10 * 2 is 20, not 5. Brackets beat everything, so use them whenever you'd have to stop and think.

int dmg = (attack - armour) * 3 / 2;   // brackets first, then left to right
Remainder, powers and negatives

% gives the remainder and only works on whole numbers. Try it on a float and it won't compile; fmodf from <math.h> does the float version.

C has no power operator. ^ exists but means something else entirely (a bit operation called XOR), so 2 ^ 3 is 1, not 8. For a square, write x * x.

With negatives, division still chops toward zero: -7 / 2 is -3. The remainder takes the sign of the left side: -7 % 2 is -1.
Dividing by zero

Write / 0 or % 0 with a literal zero and MSVC refuses to compile it (C2124). If a variable happens to be 0 at run time, whole-number division crashes the program on the spot. Float division by zero doesn't crash: it gives inf.
Two kinds of “it depends”

The C standard leaves some answers open. Implementation-defined means each compiler picks an answer and sticks to it. How many bytes an int has is one of those: 4 on yours. Undefined behaviour means the standard promises nothing at all. The program might work, print rubbish, or crash, and it can change when you change something unrelated. Dividing an int by zero is undefined. So is a number growing past what its type can hold, and so is changing a variable twice in one line, which Assignment, ++ and side effects covers. Treat undefined behaviour as a bug, even when it seems to work.
Casting to dodge overflow

An int tops out around 2.1 billion, and multiplying can get there fast. coins * 1000000 goes wrong once coins passes 2147. A cast to a bigger type fixes it, but only if it comes before the multiply, exactly like the float cast before a division:

long long total = (long long)coins * 1000000;

How big a number can be covers long long and the exact limits.

walk: Two ints declared on one line. Same as writing them separately.
int / int gives an int. 7 / 2 is 3. The .5 is thrown away, not rounded.
% is the remainder: 7 / 2 is 3 remainder 1. Handy for “every 3rd frame”, which you'll write in Decisions & Loops.
If either side is a float, the maths is done in float: 3.500000.
(float)a is a cast: “treat a as a float for this calculation”. A cast goes before the division, so it’s float / int, and you get 3.5.
The brackets run first, so the cast happens after the division. 7 / 2 is already 3, and you get 3.000000.
rungs.model: Mental model: the types going in decide the type coming out. int with int stays int. Bring one float in, with a float number or a cast, before the division happens, and the whole calculation becomes float.

check.hint: Do the part in brackets first. What is 7 / 2 in int maths?
check.why: (a / b) runs first as int maths and gives 3. Casting 3 to float gives 3.0, printed as 3.000000. The cast came too late to save the .5.

miss.1: That’s line 8, where the cast happens before the division.
miss.3: Int division throws the remainder away. It never rounds up.

tryit.task: Make this print the right percentage: 3 hits out of 4 should print 75.0.
tryit.answer: (float)   so it reads (float)hits / shots * 100. Without it, 3 / 4 is 0 and you get 0.0.

qa: Why is 3 / 4 zero?
Int division: 4 goes into 3 zero times. The 0.75 is thrown away.
What about negative numbers?
-7 / 2 is -3 in C. It chops toward zero, not down. And -7 % 2 is -1: the remainder takes the sign of the left side.
Is there a power operator?
There's no operator for it, and ^ is not it (2 ^ 3 is 1). Multiply: x * x. For anything bigger, pow in <math.h> works on doubles.
Why does my health bar stay empty?

health / max_health with two ints is 0 for every value below full. Cast first: (float)health / max_health. For a percentage, multiply first: hp * 100 / max_hp gives 25 for 30 out of 120, but hp / max_hp * 100 gives 0.
What is % good for?
It gives the leftover after dividing. n % 2 is 0 for even numbers, and (i + 1) % count wraps back to 0 at the end of a list.
rungs.bridge: You can trust your maths. Next: Assignment, ++ and side effects, the shorthand every game update uses.

rungs.title: Assignment, ++ and side effects
rungs.builds: Variables: storing a number (Phase 1): = stores a value. Division, remainder and casts: precedence, and undefined behaviour.
rungs.why: Every frame, your game changes something: the score goes up, the ammo goes down, the frame counter ticks on. C has a shorthand for exactly that, and every loop you write next phase uses it. The shorthand also hides a couple of traps that compile without a word.

parts: Assignment has a value

You already know = stores the right side in the box on the left. There's a second half: the whole assignment is also an expression, and its value is whatever was just stored. That's why combo = hits = 0; works. Assignment runs right to left, so hits = 0 happens first, its value is 0, and that 0 goes into combo.

Chaining is handy for resetting a few counters at once. Don't build longer tricks out of it; one change per line is easier to read.
Side effects and lvalues

Most operators only work out an answer. score + 5 gives 15 and changes nothing. A few operators also change a variable on the way: =, the compound ones like +=, and ++ and --. That change is called a side effect.

The left side of an assignment has to be something that can hold a value, which so far means a variable. C calls that an lvalue (the l is for left). 5 = lives; or score + 1 = 10; has no box to store into, and MSVC stops with C2106.
Compound assignment

Games are full of “take this value and change it”. C has a short form for each arithmetic operator:

score += 5;      // score = score + 5
ammo  -= 1;      // ammo = ammo - 1
speed *= 2.0f;   // speed = speed * 2.0f
timer /= 2;      // timer = timer / 2
frame %= 60;     // frame = frame % 60

The right side is worked out completely first. hp -= dmg * 2 means hp = hp - (dmg * 2). You write the name once, so there's less to mistype. They work on floats too: x += speed * dt; is the line that moves almost everything in a game.

Watch the order of the two characters. score =+ 5; is read as score = +5; and simply sets score to 5. It compiles without a word.
++ and --

lives++ adds 1 to lives and lives-- takes 1 away. Each comes in two forms, and they differ in the value they hand back:

  • Prefix, ++hits: change first, then hand over the new value.
  • Postfix, hits++: hand over the old value, then change.

With hits at 4, combo = hits++; gives combo 4 and hits 5. combo = ++hits; then gives both 6. On a line of their own, hits++; and ++hits; do exactly the same thing, because nobody uses the value handed back. ++ and -- also bind tighter than * (they go first), so 2 * lives++ doubles the old lives.
Read it or change it, not both

C doesn't fix the order in which the parts of an expression are worked out. That's fine until one part changes a variable that another part reads. Then there's no right answer:

hits = hits++;                     // undefined
printf("%d %d\n", lives, lives--); // undefined
total = n++ + n;                   // undefined

These are undefined behaviour, from Division, remainder and casts. They may print what you expect today and something else tomorrow, and MSVC won't always warn. The rule: if an expression changes a variable, don't mention that variable anywhere else in it. Split it into two lines. Changing two different variables is fine: combo = hits++; changes combo and hits once each, and reads hits only once.
Statements that do nothing

Any expression followed by ; is a legal statement, even one with no side effect. score + 5; works out 15 and throws it away; MSVC warns C4552, and under /WX that stops the build, which is good: you almost always meant score += 5;. A bare score; gets no warning at all, so that one is on you.

walk: += adds to what’s already there: score = score + 5. 10 becomes 15.
*= multiplies in place: 15 becomes 30.
-- takes 1 off. lives goes from 3 to 2.
Prints 30 2.
Postfix: hits++ hands over the old value, 4, to combo. Then hits becomes 5.
Prefix: ++hits adds 1 first (5 becomes 6), then hands over 6. Both are 6.
Assignment runs right to left. hits = 0 happens first, its value is 0, and that goes into combo.
Prints 0 0.
rungs.model: Mental model: an expression is a question with an answer. Most operators only answer. =, +=, ++ and -- answer and change a box on the way: that change is the side effect. Postfix hands over the answer from before the change; prefix hands over the one from after.

check.hint: hits++ is postfix. Which value does it hand to combo: the one from before the add, or after?
check.why: hits++ hands the old value, 4, to combo, and then adds 1 to hits. So combo is 4 and hits is 5.

miss.0: That’s what ++hits would do: change first, then hand over the new value.
miss.2: hits did go up. The ++ always happens; postfix only decides which value combo gets.
miss.3: Backwards: combo gets the old value, and hits keeps the new one.

tryit.task: Rewrite each line using compound assignment or ++/--. Then predict: if kills, ammo and damage start at 0, 30 and 5, what are they afterwards? Print them to check.
tryit.answer: kills++;   ammo -= 3;   damage *= 2;   They end at 1, 27 and 10.

qa: Is score += 5 faster than score = score + 5?
No. The compiler turns both into the same machine code. The short form is easier to read, and you only type the name once, so a long name can't be misspelled on one side.
Should I write i++ or ++i?
On a line of its own it makes no difference. Most C code uses i++ by habit. It only matters when the value is used in the same expression, and then the rule from Read it or change it applies.
Does += work on floats?
Yes, and you'll write it constantly: x += speed * dt; moves a player every frame. Only %= needs whole numbers.
Why would anyone want = to have a value?
It lets you chain resets like a = b = 0. It's also why typing = when you meant to compare still compiles, a classic bug you'll meet in Decisions with if / else (MSVC warns C4706 there).
rungs.bridge: Your maths can change things now. Last in this phase: How big a number can be, because every box has a limit.

rungs.title: How big a number can be
rungs.builds: Variables and types: int, float, double and char. Division, remainder and casts: undefined behaviour. Assignment, ++ and side effects: -- on a counter.
rungs.why: An int can't count forever. Each type has a fixed number of bytes, and that sets the biggest number it can hold. Go past the end and C doesn't stop you: the number wraps round or goes wrong. A high score, a frame counter that runs for hours and a lifetime XP total all need a type with room.

parts: Every box has a size

Each type uses a fixed number of bytes, and that sets the biggest number it can hold. Here's what you get with MSVC on 64-bit Windows:

char        1 byte    -128 to 127
short       2 bytes   about ±32 thousand
int         4 bytes   about ±2.1 billion
long        4 bytes   the same as int!
long long   8 bytes   about ±9.2 billion billion
float       4 bytes   about 6-7 digits
double      8 bytes   about 15 digits

On Windows, long is 4 bytes even in a 64-bit program. On 64-bit Linux and Mac it's 8. Code and tutorials written there often use long for big numbers, and on your PC it overflows at the same point as an int. Use long long when you need more than 2.1 billion.
signed and unsigned

Every whole-number type comes in two flavours. signed, the default, holds negatives and positives. unsigned gives up the negatives and gets twice the positive range: an unsigned int runs from 0 to 4,294,967,295. Whether a plain char is signed is up to the compiler; MSVC makes it signed.

You don't have to remember the limits. <limits.h> names them: INT_MAX, INT_MIN, UINT_MAX, LLONG_MAX and friends.
Going past the end

Unsigned numbers wrap, like a car's mileage counter. One past the top is 0, and one below 0 is the top. That's defined: it always happens the same way.

Signed overflow is undefined behaviour. INT_MAX + 1 often comes out as a large negative number, but the standard promises nothing, and an optimising compiler may assume it never happens and produce strange code around it. Don't rely on it. Pick a type with room to spare. An int frame counter at 60 frames a second reaches INT_MAX after about 414 days: fine for a play session, but not for a lifetime total.
Writing and printing the bigger types

A suffix sets a literal's type: 10u is unsigned, 10L long, 3000000000LL long long, and 2.5f float, as you know. Each type has its own printf slot:

  • %u unsigned int, %ld long, %lld long long
  • %zu the result of sizeof
  • %x an unsigned int in hexadecimal, handy for colours and bit flags later

The wrong slot is a format mismatch, so MSVC warns C4477 and /WX stops the build.
float or double?

A float holds about 6 or 7 significant digits. That's plenty for a position on screen, but it runs out: 16777217.0f is stored as 16777216, and a timer that adds 0.016f every frame for hours slowly drifts. A double holds about 15 digits. Use float for game values and double when small errors would pile up.
Mixing types

Before any maths, C quietly makes both sides the same type. char and short become int. Then the smaller type climbs to match the bigger one, roughly int, then unsigned int, then long long, then float, then double.

The trap is int meeting unsigned int: the int becomes unsigned. With unsigned int coins = 3; and int cost = 5;, coins - cost is not -2 but 4,294,967,294. When you compare signed and unsigned values in Comparisons, &&, || and !, MSVC warns C4018. Keep game values signed and this mostly goes away.
sizeof, size_t and typedef

sizeof(type) gives a size in bytes, worked out while compiling. Its result is a size_t, an unsigned type that's 8 bytes on 64-bit Windows, which is why it gets its own slot, %zu.

typedef gives an existing type a new name: typedef unsigned int Coins; lets you write Coins wallet = 0;. And <stdint.h> has types with an exact size on every computer, like int32_t and int64_t, for when the size really matters. You'll see typedef again when you name your own struct types in Phase 3.5.

walk: limits.h names the biggest and smallest value of each type, like INT_MAX.
sizeof gives a size in bytes. Its result is a size_t, and %zu is its printf slot. An int is 4 bytes.
long is also 4 bytes on Windows, even in a 64-bit program. On Linux and Mac it’s 8.
INT_MAX is 2147483647, the top of an int.
3 billion fits neither an int nor a Windows long. The LL suffix makes the number a long long.
%lld is the slot for a long long.
An unsigned int can’t go below 0, so 0 minus 1 wraps round to the top: 4294967295.
%x prints the same number in hexadecimal: ffffffff. Every bit is 1.
rungs.model: Mental model: a mileage counter with a fixed number of wheels. The type decides how many wheels you get. Roll past the last number and an unsigned counter starts again from 0; a signed one does something C won't promise.

check.hint: An unsigned int can’t go below 0. Picture a mileage counter rolling backwards.
check.why: Unsigned numbers wrap. One below 0 is the biggest value an unsigned int holds, 4294967295 (UINT_MAX). That’s defined behaviour, unlike signed overflow.

miss.0: An unsigned int has no room for -1, and %u prints it as unsigned anyway.
miss.1: C doesn’t stop at 0. It wraps round to the top.
miss.3: Unsigned wrap is fully defined: no crash and no warning.

qa: Why %zu for sizeof? Doesn’t %d work?
sizeof gives a size_t, which on 64-bit Windows is an 8-byte unsigned number. %d expects a 4-byte int, so MSVC warns C4477 and /WX stops the build. Use %zu, or cast it: (int)sizeof(x) with %d.
A tutorial says long is 8 bytes. Who’s right?
Both. On 64-bit Linux and Mac it’s 8; on Windows it’s 4, even in 64-bit programs. For anything past 2.1 billion use long long, or int64_t from <stdint.h>.
Scores can’t be negative. Should they be unsigned?

Usually not. Unsigned maths wraps without a sound: lives - 1 at 0 becomes about 4 billion. Mixing unsigned with int also changes the results of comparisons. Keep game values as int; unsigned is for sizes, colours and bit flags.
How long until a frame counter overflows?
At 60 frames a second an int lasts about 414 days, so it's fine for a game session. A long long would last billions of years.
